content:
The first thing I learned about working with Team Avatar was that legends were terrible at keeping meeting times.

Katara arrived early.

Toph arrived exactly when she meant to and claimed that made her punctual.

Aang arrived through the window.

The council clerk did not appreciate this.

“You know,” I said while Aang untangled the hem of his robes from a potted tree, “there is a door.”

“I saw it.”

“And rejected it on principle?”

“The window was closer.”

Toph leaned back in her chair. “He’s been like this since he was twelve.”

Katara slid a stack of reports toward Aang. “And somehow the world let him stay this way.”

Their affection was obvious in the way old roads were obvious: worn smooth by years of use. Katara did not have to look at Aang to know he would steal the fruit from her breakfast plate. She slapped his fingers without interrupting her sentence. He grinned and took the fruit from Toph instead.

Toph bit him.

Not hard.

Probably.

I had been invited to the planning session because, as Aang put it, I had “the terrifying ability to know where all the bodies are buried in the filing system.” I had corrected him that no bodies were buried in the filing system.

“Yet,” Toph had said.

The meeting itself was less funny.

Cranefish Town was growing so quickly that no one could agree on who had authority over what. Earth Kingdom officials wanted old property lines honored. Fire Nation families who had lived there for generations refused to be treated like temporary colonists. New arrivals needed housing. Factory owners wanted fewer inspections. Workers wanted to stop losing fingers.

Aang stood at the front of the room with a map spread behind him.

“We can’t build peace by deciding one group belongs more than another,” he said.

It was a good sentence.

It was also not a sewer plan.

A merchant representative raised his hand. “Then the Avatar agrees that the western expansion should proceed.”

“I agree that families need homes.”

“With respect, Avatar Aang, that is not an answer.”

Aang’s jaw tightened.

Katara noticed. So did Toph. So did I.

The merchant continued, “If we wait for every district to settle every grievance, nothing will be built.”

“And if we build without settling any of them,” I said, “we’ll put three hundred people on land with one water line and no waste channel.”

Every head in the room turned.

I regretted speaking for approximately half a heartbeat.

Then Katara said, “They’re right.”

The merchant frowned. “And you are?”

“Someone who has the numbers.”

He looked at my plain clothes, my ink-stained fingers, and the lack of any bending insignia.

“I was asking your title.”

“I don’t have one.”

Toph smiled like a shark.

“Best title in the room,” she said.

The argument lasted two hours.

Aang wanted consensus. Katara wanted protections written before construction began. Toph wanted the factory owners to stop lying. I wanted everyone to stop saying “mixed-use civic corridor” when they meant “a road with shops on it.”

By the time the council broke for tea, I had a headache behind my left eye.

I escaped to the balcony.

Cranefish Town spread below in afternoon haze. Hammers rang from a construction site. Somewhere a street vendor yelled about dumplings.

“You were angry.”

Aang’s voice came from behind me.

I looked over my shoulder. “That narrows it down.”

“At me.”

He stepped beside me but left enough space that I did not feel cornered.

I considered lying.

Then remembered Toph was fifteen feet away and would probably shout about it.

“You talk about harmony like everyone in the room wants the same thing,” I said.

Aang rested his forearms on the railing. “They don’t.”

“You act like they might if you explain it well enough.”

He was quiet.

The wind tugged at the loose edge of his sleeve.

“I used to think if people understood each other, they would stop hurting each other,” he said.

“Used to?”

“I’m trying to stop.”

That answer took some of the fight out of me.

Aang looked down at the street. “Air Nomads were taught to move around obstacles. Find another path. Redirect. Let anger pass through without becoming it.”

“Toph must have loved teaching you earthbending.”

He laughed softly. “She put me in front of a boulder and yelled until I got mad enough to stand my ground.”

“That sounds like her.”

“It was awful.”

“You adore her.”

The words came out before I thought about them.

Aang’s expression shifted.

Not embarrassed. Not exactly.

Soft.

“Yes,” he said.

The simplicity of it caught me off guard.

Inside the room, Toph was arguing with someone about structural load. Katara’s voice cut through the noise, calm but firm.

Aang glanced back toward them.

“I love Katara,” he said. “That’s not complicated.”

“No?”

“The loving part isn’t.” He smiled faintly. “The being two people with responsibilities, tempers, bad habits, and friends who walk into your room without knocking part can get complicated.”

“Toph doesn’t knock?”

“Toph says doors are a visual people problem.”

I laughed.

Aang’s smile widened, but then he looked at me with an openness that made my pulse trip.

“You don’t have to agree with me because I’m the Avatar.”

“I had gathered that.”

“I mean it.”

“I know.”

His gaze stayed on mine for a second longer than necessary.

I looked away first.

Katara appeared in the doorway carrying two cups. “There you are.”

Her eyes moved between us, reading the air with an accuracy that had nothing to do with bending.

“Am I interrupting?”

“No,” I said too quickly.

Aang said, “Maybe.”

I stared at him.

He grinned.

Katara handed me one cup. “He does that when he thinks someone is cute.”

My entire mind stopped.

Aang made a noise of betrayal. “Katara!”

“What?” She took a sip from her own cup. “You do.”

From inside the chamber, Toph yelled, “Heartbeat says Paperwork knows!”

I considered climbing over the balcony rail.

Aang looked delighted.

Katara looked amused.

Toph, apparently, had become the worst person alive.

“I’m going home,” I said.

“No, you’re not,” Katara replied. “We haven’t finished the drainage plan.”

I looked at her.

She looked back, utterly composed.

Then the corner of her mouth lifted.

It was the first time I realized Katara could be dangerous without moving a drop of water.

The meeting resumed.

Something had changed, though only by a degree.

Aang listened more when the workers spoke. When he started to smooth over a disagreement too quickly, he caught himself and asked another question. Katara stopped one councilman from volunteering me for six weeks of unpaid work. Toph kicked my chair whenever she sensed me trying not to laugh.

By sunset, we had an actual plan: housing could expand, but only after the city funded water, waste, and firebreaks first. Inspections would include a worker representative. Injury reports would go to an independent office instead of factory owners.

It was not harmony.

It was compromise held together by ink.

Outside, Aang stretched his arms over his head. “Dinner?”

“Is that a meeting?” I asked.

“No.”

“Will there be documents?”

“No.”

Toph walked past us. “Katara made lists.”

Aang sighed. “There may be documents.”

Katara shoved Toph lightly with one shoulder. “It’s a grocery list.”

“See?” Toph said. “Paperwork.”

I should have gone home.

Instead I followed them down the steps and into the evening crowd.

Aang walked beside me. Katara linked her arm through his on the other side. Toph moved ahead of us barefoot, tapping the street once with every few steps as if the city were speaking up through the soles of her feet.

I had spent the day earning a seat at a council table.

It was ridiculous that the place I noticed most was the one opening beside them.

That evening, I found the meeting notes folded beneath my door with three additions in three different hands.

Katara had corrected the location of the temporary clinic and added a reminder that the eastern wells needed testing before another family was moved into the district. Aang had drawn a tiny arrow beside the paragraph about the children’s courtyard and written, Ask them what they want, not only what adults think they need. Toph’s contribution was a hard, angular line under the section about accessible streets, followed by: STOP BUILDING STAIRS LIKE EVERYONE HAS LEGS MADE OF SPRINGS.

I sat on the edge of my bed laughing until the room stopped feeling empty.

Under Toph’s note, in smaller writing that could only have been Katara’s, someone had added, She means ramps and level entrances.

Beneath that, Aang had written, She definitely also means the stairs.

I took out my pen and added a fourth note.

I’ll ask the people who use them.

The next morning, Toph took the papers from my hands, ran her thumb over the crease, and grinned.

“Look at that,” she said. “Council person learned something.”

“I’m not a council person.”

“Keep hanging around us. Somebody will give you a title eventually.”

Aang groaned as if this were a genuine threat. Katara smiled over her tea.

For once, I did not mind the possibility.
